paragraphs.title: Asa Establishes the Worship of the Lord and Strengthens the Kingdom

answers: He did that which was good and right
He built temples for foreign gods
easy.explanation: Asa did that which was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God.
easy.q: How is Asa described at the beginning of the passage?

answers: The altars of the strange gods and the high places
easy.explanation: Asa removed the altars of the strange gods, the high places, the images, and the groves.
easy.q: What did Asa take away from Judah?

answers: Seek the LORD and do the law and the commandment
easy.explanation: Asa commanded Judah to seek the LORD God of their fathers and to do the law and the commandment.
easy.q: What did Asa command Judah to do?

answers: The land had rest and there was no war
medium.explanation: The land had rest, and Asa had no war in those years.
medium.q: What enabled Judah to build fenced cities?

answers: War, removal of the high places, and then prayer
Removal of idolatry, seeking the LORD, and building fenced cities
Building cities, abandoning the law, and removing the walls
medium.explanation: Asa removed idolatrous objects, encouraged the people to seek the LORD, and built fortified cities.
medium.q: Which sequence of actions is described in the passage?

medium.explanation: The statement means that the kingdom was in a peaceful condition.
medium.q: What does the statement “the kingdom was quiet before him” mean?

answers: It connects seeking the LORD, rest from enemies, and successful building
It says the building succeeded despite forsaking the LORD
It says the Ethiopians built the cities
challenge.explanation: Asa says they sought the LORD, and He gave them rest on every side; therefore they built and prospered.
challenge.q: What connection does the passage make between seeking the LORD and building the cities?

answers: They were built beside the sea
They had walls, towers, gates, and bars
challenge.explanation: Walls, towers, gates, and bars are defensive features.
challenge.q: Which detail shows that the cities were intended for defense?

answers: Asa focused only on military construction
Asa strengthened both faithfulness to God and the defense of the land
challenge.explanation: The passage describes both removing idolatry and seeking the LORD, as well as building fortified cities.
challenge.q: What is the significance of combining religious reform with preparation of the kingdom?

easy.explanation: Judah had three hundred thousand men bearing targets and spears.
easy.q: How many men were from Judah?

easy.explanation: Benjamin had men that bare shields and drew bows.
easy.q: What did the warriors from Benjamin carry?

easy.explanation: The verse concludes, “all these were mighty men of valour.”
easy.q: How are all the soldiers described?

answers: Judah carried targets and spears, while Benjamin carried shields and bows
Judah rode chariots, while Benjamin carried sheep
Judah had no weapons, while Benjamin built walls
medium.explanation: The verse identifies the different weapons carried by the two tribes.
medium.q: What was the main difference between the forces of Judah and Benjamin?

medium.explanation: Three hundred thousand plus two hundred eighty thousand equals five hundred eighty thousand.
medium.q: What was the total number of soldiers from Judah and Benjamin?

medium.explanation: The expression describes soldiers who were courageous and capable.
medium.q: What does “mighty men of valour” mean in this context?

answers: It included both spear bearers and bowmen
It included only soldiers without weapons
challenge.explanation: The verse mentions men carrying spears and men drawing bows.
challenge.q: Which detail emphasizes the variety of Asa’s army?

challenge.explanation: The men of Benjamin are described as those that drew bows.
challenge.q: Which tribe is specifically described as drawing bows?

answers: The army was large, organized, and made up of different units
The army was unprepared for defense
The army consisted only of people from one city
challenge.explanation: The details about numbers, tribes, and weapons present a large and organized army.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the numbers and equipment listed for the army?

paragraphs.title: The Encounter with Zerah the Ethiopian and Asa’s Prayer

answers: One of the kings of Judah
easy.explanation: Zerah the Ethiopian came against Judah with a great host.
easy.q: Who came to Mareshah with a great host?

answers: In the valley of Zephathah at Mareshah
easy.explanation: Asa and his army set the battle in array in the valley of Zephathah at Mareshah.
easy.q: Where was the battle set in array?

easy.explanation: Asa cried unto the LORD his God and asked for His help.

answers: A thousand thousand men and three hundred chariots
Three hundred thousand men without chariots
medium.explanation: Zerah came with a host of a thousand thousand and three hundred chariots.
medium.q: How large was Zerah’s army according to the passage?

answers: Help Judah against the multitude, although Judah had little power
Send the Ethiopians back to Mareshah
medium.explanation: Asa asked God to help them even though they had no power compared with the multitude.
medium.q: What did Asa ask the LORD to do?

answers: Whether facing a great army or having little strength
medium.explanation: Asa declares that the LORD can help whether His people are many or have little power.
medium.q: What does “whether with many, or with them that have no power” mean?

answers: God’s help is not limited to situations in which the armies are equal
Only a great army can win
There is no need to ask for help before a battle
challenge.explanation: Asa asks God to help Judah even though they are greatly outnumbered.
challenge.q: What belief is expressed in Asa’s prayer?

answers: The difference between two peaceful cities
Zerah’s enormous army contrasted with Asa’s prayer and trust in the LORD
The difference between two kinds of gates
challenge.explanation: The passage highlights the size of Zerah’s army and Asa’s dependence on God.
challenge.q: What creates the main contrast in the description of the conflict?

answers: The battle was in the valley of Zephathah near Mareshah
The Ethiopians reached only as far as Gerar
challenge.explanation: The passage says that the battle was set in the valley of Zephathah at Mareshah.
challenge.q: What geographical detail identifies the place of the battle?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “So the LORD smote the Ethiopians.”
easy.q: Who smote the Ethiopians before Asa and Judah?

easy.explanation: Asa and the people with him pursued the Ethiopians unto Gerar.
easy.q: How far did Asa and his people pursue the Ethiopians?

answers: Very much spoil, including sheep and camels
easy.explanation: They carried away very much spoil, including sheep and camels in abundance.
easy.q: What did Judah carry away from the region?

answers: They pursued them, smote the cities around Gerar, and took spoil
They built fenced cities at Mareshah
medium.explanation: They pursued the Ethiopians, smote the surrounding cities, and spoiled them.
medium.q: What did the men of Judah do after the Ethiopians fled?

answers: The fear of the LORD came upon them
medium.explanation: The passage states that the fear of the LORD came upon them.
medium.q: Why did the cities around Gerar not withstand Judah?

answers: They had no place to live
They could not regain strength or recover from the defeat
medium.explanation: The phrase means that the Ethiopians could not recover after being overthrown.
medium.q: What does “they could not recover themselves” mean?

answers: The LORD smote the Ethiopians, and afterward Judah pursued them
Judah won without any mention of God’s intervention
The cities around Gerar defeated the Ethiopians
challenge.explanation: First the LORD smote the Ethiopians, and then Asa and his people pursued them.
challenge.q: How does the sequence of the verses describe the source of the victory?

answers: The pursuit ended with a return after victory and the gathering of spoil
Asa moved his throne to Gerar
The army was defeated and returned without possessions
challenge.explanation: After the victory and gathering of spoil, Asa and his people returned to Jerusalem.
challenge.q: What does the return to Jerusalem at the end of the passage show?

answers: Judah smote the cities around Gerar and the tents of cattle
Judah fought only in the valley of Zephathah
challenge.explanation: The passage describes attacks on surrounding cities and cattle tents, along with the taking of sheep and camels.
challenge.q: Which detail shows that the victory extended beyond the main battlefield?
